claims.text: Wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by an in-situ-formed protective oxide tribolayer.
A stable protective oxide tribolayer forms when a reactive element such as Cr or Al exceeds a critical alloy concentration.
The baseline coating has a reactive-element concentration below the critical concentration for optimal tribolayer formation.
Reactive-element content will be systematically varied across concentrations below and above the anticipated critical concentration.
Wear tests will be performed at ambient temperature with load and sliding speed controlled.
SEM/EDS and XPS can be used after testing to assess oxide-tribolayer formation and composition.
Increasing reactive-element content promotes tribo-oxidation during sliding.
Increasing reactive-element content causes rapid formation and stabilization of the protective oxide layer.
The oxide tribolayer acts as a lubricant.
The oxide tribolayer provides a barrier against direct metal-to-metal contact.
Formation of the oxide tribolayer reduces wear rate.
Formation of the oxide tribolayer reduces the friction coefficient.
Coatings below the critical reactive-element concentration fail to form a continuous protective oxide layer.
Crossing the critical reactive-element concentration will produce a clear transition to a stable tribolayer, lower wear rate, and lower friction coefficient.
Below-threshold coatings exhibit minimal tribolayer formation and consequently higher wear rates and friction coefficients.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold at ambient temperature under fixed load and sliding speed.
Applicability at elevated temperature or substantially different sliding conditions is uncertain.
The exact critical concentration and magnitude of wear improvement are undetermined and may depend on test conditions.
The hypothesis is falsified if increasing reactive-element content produces neither a transition to lower wear and friction nor formation of a protective oxide tribolayer.
